messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai is a 24-year-old painter who lives with his girlfriend in a small apartment on the outskirts of a midsized city. He came to therapy at her urging, after months of what she described as him "living like a ghost." The event that fractured his life happened eighteen months ago, when he was still living with his previous partner, a man named Derek. What began as verbal jabs during arguments escalated one night into Derek shoving him against a wall, then pinning him to the floor with a knee on his chest while screaming inches from his face. Kai remembers the pressure in his ribs, the spit on his cheek, and then nothing—a complete blank where the next several minutes should be. Other moments from that night, like the sound of a lamp shattering or the sight of his own hand gripping the carpet, are burned into his mind with excruciating clarity, but he cannot arrange them in any order that makes sense. The gaps terrify him more than the images do, because he is certain that what he cannot remember must be the worst part.

In the months that followed, Kai found himself unable to shake the feeling that he was fundamentally the kind of person this happens to. He had always struggled with a quiet sense of inadequacy, but now it crystallized into a fixed belief: the event happened because of who he was, and that meant he no longer belonged anywhere—not in his old life, not in his new relationship, not even in his own body. This conviction colored everything. When his girlfriend would ask him a simple question, he would feel a spike of dread, certain she was about to see through him. He began to notice that any moment of uncertainty—a text left unread, a delay in her response—triggered a cascade of unwanted thoughts about Derek finding him again. The uncertainty itself became a trigger, and soon he was scanning for exits the moment he entered any room, listening for footsteps at the door, and interpreting any delay as evidence that something terrible was unfolding just out of sight. The more he believed he was inadequate and did not belong, the more he watched for threats, and the more he watched, the more triggers he found.

The triggers, in turn, fed back into his memory. A sudden silence in the apartment would drop him straight back into that night, reliving the pressure on his chest as if it were happening right then. The reliving episodes were disorienting and fragmented, and each one deepened his confusion about what had actually happened, which made him feel even more broken and worthless. He started avoiding anything that reminded him of Derek—certain streets, the time of evening when the attack had occurred, even the smell of a particular cologne. He also began to freeze completely when he felt threatened, unable to move or speak, which only reinforced his sense of inadequacy. These strategies, meant to protect him, actually made things worse: avoiding triggers meant he never tested his fears, so the memories stayed raw and unpredictable, and freezing left him feeling humiliated and even more convinced that he was the sort of person who deserved what happened.

The cycle tightened. Every time he froze, the memory of the attack felt more vivid and more out of his control. Every time he scanned for exits, he noticed new potential threats, which triggered more intrusive thoughts, which sent him back into the fragmented reliving. He began to monitor for sounds of someone entering the apartment obsessively, and this hypervigilance made him irritable and exhausted. His girlfriend started to feel like she was walking on eggshells, and Kai, noticing her hesitation, interpreted it as proof that he no longer belonged in this relationship either. The strategies that were supposed to keep him safe were, in his mind, the very things that confirmed he was broken.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at work. He was painting a ceiling in a client's living room when the homeowner, a large man, walked in without warning. Kai dropped his roller, scrambled down the ladder, and stood frozen in the corner, unable to speak or move for nearly a minute. The man was apologetic, confused, and eventually concerned. Kai drove home shaking, and that night he told his girlfriend he could not keep living this way. He is afraid that he will never feel safe again, and that the person he was before the attack is gone for good. But beneath that, in the quietest part of himself, he is most afraid that his worst appraisal is correct—that the event happened because of who he is, and that no amount of therapy can change that.
